extracted.intended_audience: patent applicants, PTAB practitioners, and appellate counsel
extracted.subtask_description: Legal standards and procedural criteria governing requests for Director review of PTAB/ex parte decisions, timeliness/forfeiture of Appointments Clause challenges, and when agencies may reopen final decisions after an appellate mandate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Director review authority under Arthrex
rubrics_metrics.description: The Director has the authority to provide for a means of reviewing PTAB decisions and accordingly may review final PTAB decisions and, upon review, may issue decisions himself on behalf of the Board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the Supreme Court's remedy for an Appointments Clause violation in Arthrex (594 U.S. at 25). The Director's review power serves as an available remedy for constitutional defects in APJs' authority; it is distinct from remedies fashioned by the Federal Circuit.

rubrics_metrics.name: PTO interim process scope — no Director review for ex parte appeals
rubrics_metrics.description: At this time, the Office does not accept requests for Director review of . . . ex parte appeal decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Per the PTO's interim process for Director review §8 ("Scope of Review"), the PTO may decline to consider Director-review requests that fall outside its stated scope (e.g., ex parte appeal decisions). A request outside the scope will not be considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finality after appellate mandate (MPEP §1216.01)
rubrics_metrics.description: Once this court has affirmed the rejection of a patent application's claims, the 'proceedings in the case are considered terminated on the issue date of the . . . mandate.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An affirmative appellate mandate generally renders the Board's decision final for agency purposes; requests to reopen or reconsider are therefore treated as requests to reopen a final decision rather than continuation of active proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agencies possess inherent authority to reconsider decisions, subject to limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative agencies possess inherent authority to reconsider their decisions, subject to certain limitations, regardless of whether they possess explicit statutory authority to do so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The PTO (and other agencies) may reopen final decisions based on inherent authority (Tokyo Kikai Seisakusho v. United States and related cases), but that authority is limited by doctrines such as 'reasonable time' and other equitable constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconsideration must occur within a reasonable time
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency's reconsideration 'must occur within a reasonable time.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts evaluate reasonableness case-by-case (Tokyo Kikai Seisakusho, Macktal, Bookman). Excessive delay may render reconsideration improper; 'short and reasonable time period' language is used to describe the expectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 60(b)(6) is a useful analogue for agency reopening
rubrics_metrics.description: Principles animating Rule 60(b), especially Rule 60(b)(6) (relief for 'any other reason that justifies relief'), can guide the scope of an agency's inherent power to reconsider prior decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule 60(b)(6) relief requires extraordinary circumstances and that the motion be made within a reasonable time (Fed. R. Civ. P. 60(c)(1)). Intervening developments in law by themselves rarely suffice as 'extraordinary circumstances' (Gonzalez v. Crosby; Agostini). Courts have, however, made narrow exceptions where diligence and unusual equities exist (e.g., Bynoe, In re Terrorist Attacks).

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness for Rule 60(b)(6) is measured from when grounds are available
rubrics_metrics.description: When a Rule 60(b)(6) motion is premised on a change in law, courts measure timeliness 'as of the point in time when the moving party has grounds to make [a Rule 60(b)] motion, regardless of the time that has elapsed since the entry of judgment.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This standard (quoting Bynoe and Clark) focuses on when the movant knew or should have known of the grounds for relief; delay after that point weighs against relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forfeiture of Appointments Clause challenges when not raised on direct review
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure to raise an Appointments Clause challenge in an opening brief (or on direct appeal) constitutes forfeiture, even when the argument existed or was raised before the termination of the appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Federal Circuit has repeatedly held that failing to present the Appointments Clause argument in the first appeal results in forfeiture (e.g., Ciena Corp., Customedia Techs., Sanofi-Aventis, Vivint). Forfeiture can be excused only in narrow circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appointments Clause challenges are not jurisdictional
rubrics_metrics.description: An Appointments Clause challenge is not jurisdictional and must be timely presented and preserved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the challenge is non-jurisdictional, courts treat failure to raise it as forfeiture (which may be excused in exceptional cases), not as a lack of subject-matter jurisdiction (see Customedia; Micron discussion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Diligence factors that bear on excusing forfeiture
rubrics_metrics.description: A court assessing whether to excuse forfeiture will consider the moving party's diligence—e.g., whether the party failed to raise the issue before the district court, declined to file an appeal or petition for rehearing, or neglected to seek certiorari.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lack of diligence is a strong reason to deny Rule 60(b)(6) relief (FTC v. Hewitt and other circuit decisions). By contrast, courts have granted relief in rare cases where a movant promptly pursued its claim and acted diligently (e.g., Bynoe).

rubrics_metrics.name: Change in law rarely constitutes extraordinary circumstances; limited exception when prior precedent precluded objection
rubrics_metrics.description: Intervening developments in the law by themselves rarely constitute the extraordinary circumstances required for Rule 60(b)(6) relief; forfeiture may be set aside due to change in law only in the limited circumstance in which controlling precedent precluded the district court from adopting an objection before the Supreme Court issued its decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Per Gonzalez, Agostini, and Micron, a mere change in law (e.g., Arthrex) does not automatically excuse a party's delay unless earlier controlling precedent prevented raising the claim; Odyssey's situation did not meet that narrow exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reopening after an appellate mandate limited by scope of the mandate
rubrics_metrics.description: A district court may reopen a final judgment even after issuance of an appellate mandate, provided that the relief does not fall within the scope of that mandate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard Oil Co. v. United States permits reopening only when the requested relief is outside the scope of the appellate mandate; this constrains post-mandate Rule 60-type relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abuse-of-discretion review for agency denial of reconsideration or Director review
rubrics_metrics.description: A court will affirm an agency's denial of a request for reconsideration/Director review unless the PTO abused its discretion in doing so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors supporting denial include the moving party's knowledge of the issue during the original proceedings or appeal and an unexplained delay in seeking review. Where the movant fails to justify delay or diligence, the PTO's denial is not an abuse of discretion and will be affirmed.
